title: Data model
summary: Choose entities, keys, and access paths before choosing a database product.

parts.rule: Name entities, primary keys, and the queries that must be fast. Design access paths first — lookup by code, list by user_id ordered by time — then pick a store that matches those paths. Product brand names come after the path story. Secondary indexes speed reads and slow writes; say that cost out loud when you add one.
parts.why: Starting with a vendor logo hides whether the query pattern fits. Interviewers want keys and cardinality. A model that cannot answer the primary read without a full scan is a failed design no matter which database brand is on the box.
parts.example: URL shortener entity Link: code as primary key (seven characters), long_url, owner_id, created_at. Access path one: get long_url by code — primary key lookup. Access path two: list codes by owner_id — secondary index or a separate owner-to-codes table. Cardinality around one hundred million links; a sixty-two-symbol seven-character space is vast, so random codes rarely collide. Do not pick a document store only for flexibility when every query is primary key or owner list. For chat, Message keyed by (chat_id, timestamp) serves "latest fifty messages in this chat" by range scan. A primary key on message_id alone would force a secondary index for the hot path and can create hot partitions on popular chats. Hold the method and the cost in mind before naming a tool.
parts.use: Model data immediately after the API. Write the top three queries beside the entities. Choose relational versus wide-column versus object storage from those queries and their cardinality estimates.
parts.refuse: Refuse naming a database vendor before keys exist. Refuse a model with no primary access path for the hottest read. Refuse indexing every column just in case. Refuse storing large blobs inside the transactional row when an object store fits better.

body:
Rule. Name entities, primary keys, and the queries that must be fast. Design access paths first — lookup by code, list by user_id ordered by time — then pick a store that matches those paths. Product brand names come after the path story. Secondary indexes speed reads and slow writes; say that cost out loud when you add one.

Why it matters. Starting with a vendor logo hides whether the query pattern fits. Interviewers want keys and cardinality. A model that cannot answer the primary read without a full scan is a failed design no matter which database brand is on the box.

Worked example. URL shortener entity Link: code as primary key (seven characters), long_url, owner_id, created_at. Access path one: get long_url by code — primary key lookup. Access path two: list codes by owner_id — secondary index or a separate owner-to-codes table. Cardinality around one hundred million links; a sixty-two-symbol seven-character space is vast, so random codes rarely collide. Do not pick a document store only for flexibility when every query is primary key or owner list. For chat, Message keyed by (chat_id, timestamp) serves "latest fifty messages in this chat" by range scan. A primary key on message_id alone would force a secondary index for the hot path and can create hot partitions on popular chats. Hold the method and the cost in mind before naming a tool.

When to use. Model data immediately after the API. Write the top three queries beside the entities. Choose relational versus wide-column versus object storage from those queries and their cardinality estimates.

When to refuse. Refuse naming a database vendor before keys exist. Refuse a model with no primary access path for the hottest read. Refuse indexing every column just in case. Refuse storing large blobs inside the transactional row when an object store fits better.
